name: Furosemide
lead: Furosemide, sold as Lasix and under many other brand names, is a prescription loop diuretic: a tablet, solution or injection that makes the kidneys pass large amounts of salt and water. It is used to treat fluid build-up (oedema) from heart failure, cirrhosis and kidney disease, and sometimes high blood pressure.[1][12] It was patented in 1959, approved for medical use in 1964, sits on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines and was the 29th most prescribed drug in the United States in 2023.[1]

In appearance culture the interest is in what that fluid loss does to the way a body or face reads. Bodybuilders have long manipulated water and electrolytes in the final days before a show to make skin look thinner and muscle outlines sharper, and diuretic use in that setting is described in the sports-science literature.[15][14] On looksmax.org, members use the name 'hollow cheek pill' for furosemide, describing a faster-than-diet way to remove facial puffiness, reduce under-eye fullness and make cheekbones and jaw look more defined for a photo or event.[16][22] The chain proponents describe is: less extracellular water, then less soft-tissue swelling, then sharper-looking facial and body contours for a short period.

Research on furosemide concerns patients with fluid overload, not cosmetic use. Large trials have compared dosing strategies, combination regimens and alternative loop diuretics in heart failure.[10][9][5] The US label carries a prominent warning that furosemide is a potent diuretic which, if given in excessive amounts, can lead to profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion, and that careful medical supervision is required.[12] Furosemide is also on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list because it can mask other drugs.[1] No trial has examined it for facial slimming or physique conditioning, although sports-medicine reviews describe the wider practice of pre-contest dehydration and discuss its kidney and electrolyte risks.[15][14]

chain: Blocks salt reabsorption in the kidney
Urine volume rises and extracellular water falls
Less puffiness around the face and under the eyes
Sharper-looking cheekbones, jaw and muscle outlines for a short time
angle.text: People who use furosemide for their looks are chasing a temporary 'drier' appearance: less water under the skin of the face and body, so bone structure and muscle separation look more pronounced. The effect lasts only as long as the fluid shift, which is why it is discussed for specific events or photos rather than as a lasting change.

infobox: Within 1 hour orally; about 5 minutes intravenously[1]

paras: Furosemide is mainly used for oedema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis and renal disease including nephrotic syndrome, and for hypertension when thiazides are inadequate or kidney or heart impairment is present.[12][1] It is often viewed as first-line for oedema in heart failure.[1] It is also used in adjunct therapy for brain or lung oedema where rapid diuresis is needed, and for severe hypercalcaemia with rehydration.[1] In nephrotic syndrome and hypoalbuminaemia it is sometimes combined with albumin.[1][3]

Furosemide is used in horses to reduce exercise-induced pulmonary haemorrhage; its race-day effect was found accidentally in the early 1970s, and New York became the last US state to approve it in 1995.[1] Its use is permitted in some US racing jurisdictions and prohibited in many other countries, and major US tracks ban race-day use.[1] It is also used in dogs and cats for congestive heart failure.[1]

Appearance use falls into two overlapping settings. In physique sport, competitors adjust water, sodium and carbohydrate in the final days before a contest to change how smooth or 'full' the muscles look; a 2021 review of peak-week practices describes manipulation of water and electrolyte intake aimed at reducing subcutaneous water and abdominal bloating, and notes that evidence supporting these routines is scarce.[15] An observational study of ten amateur Brazilian bodybuilders followed through peak week recorded high diuretic and other drug use under one coach; the authors report that athletes still lost lean-mass markers, which they linked to heavy aerobic work and calorie restriction.[15]

In looksmaxxing communities the interest is in the face. Members describe furosemide as a way to remove puffiness around the cheeks and eyes so that leanness already built through low body fat shows more clearly; posters say it is most relevant for people who are already lean.[16][22] A first-person 2026 thread by a user at roughly 8 percent body fat reports hollow-looking cheeks within about an hour and a drawn look around the eyes, and the author says it works while noting that it is notorious on the forum.[16][17] Other threads cover supply, side effects, comparisons with other diuretics and 'rate me' posts showing before-and-after photos.[18][21][24][31] Any change in appearance reflects fluid loss rather than fat, bone or muscle change, and ends as the body rehydrates.[12][1]

In patients with acute decompensated heart failure, the DOSE trial randomised 308 patients to intravenous furosemide by bolus or continuous infusion, at low or high dose, to compare symptom relief and kidney function.[10] Other trials have tested ways to increase diuretic response: adding a thiazide diuretic (the CLOROTIC trial used hydrochlorothiazide, with weight change and dyspnoea at 72 hours as coprimary endpoints), co-administering albumin, or giving hypertonic saline with the furosemide.[9][3][4] The TRANSFORM-HF randomised trial compared torsemide with furosemide after discharge for heart failure and measured all-cause mortality.[5]

Trials of furosemide for other purposes include postpartum blood-pressure recovery in preeclampsia and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, safety in preterm infants at risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and treatment of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis.[7][28][8][29] These studies measure clinical outcomes such as weight, blood pressure, symptoms and sodium levels, not facial or physique appearance.

Common effects include orthostatic hypotension and lightheadedness, tinnitus and photosensitivity; serious effects include electrolyte abnormalities, low blood pressure and hearing loss.[1] Electrolyte disturbances can include hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia, and gout from hyperuricaemia and hyperglycaemia may occur.[1] Furosemide is associated with ototoxicity in post-marketing reports and observational studies, although age is a major confounding risk factor.[1] Long-term use in heart failure has been associated with thiamine deficiency.[1] It can cause kidney injury, usually by dehydration and usually reversible; sulfonamide allergy is a precaution.[1] In infants, furosemide use is associated with nephrocalcinosis.[6]

The label lists numerous gastrointestinal, hypersensitivity and other reactions, and it has been shown to cause unexplained maternal deaths and abortions in rabbits at multiples of the maximum human dose; no adequate studies exist in pregnant women.[12] Interactions include NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, antiarrhythmics and other diuretics.[1] The Wikipedia article and label both stress monitoring of electrolytes and renal function.

Sports-medicine and nephrology reviews single out dehydrating practices, including diuretic misuse, as carrying potential kidney risk for bodybuilders, alongside anabolic steroids and anti-inflammatory painkillers; a 2022 review lists acute kidney injury and nephrocalcinosis among the concerns.[15] A 2021 case report describes a 32-year-old bodybuilder with severe leg weakness and a potassium level of 1.9 mmol/L three days after a contest; toxicology ruled out diuretics but detected clenbuterol, and the report describes thyroxine and other agents taken before the contest; it is an example of severe potassium depletion in the context of contest weight-making.[15] Reviews of furosemide ototoxicity describe hearing effects as a recognised, mostly dose- and rate-related risk.[27]

Furosemide blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, so sodium, chloride and potassium stay in the urine and water follows.[1][26] By disrupting potassium recycling it also reduces the voltage gradient that drives magnesium and calcium reabsorption, which explains urinary losses of those minerals, and it prevents the kidney building a concentrated medulla, so less water is reclaimed from the collecting duct.[26] The effect on the distal tubules is independent of carbonic anhydrase or aldosterone.[1] Furosemide also blocks certain GABA-A receptor subtypes in laboratory studies, which is unrelated to its diuretic action.[1]

Oral furosemide acts within about an hour and diuresis is generally complete within six to eight hours, with substantial variation between people; after intravenous injection the peak effect arrives within about 30 minutes.[1] Bioavailability by mouth is roughly 47 to 70 percent, it is cleared mainly by tubular secretion in the kidney, and clearance falls in kidney impairment.[1] The short, sharp time course is part of why forum users describe the facial effect as appearing within hours and fading the next day.[16]

Furosemide is a prescription medicine in the United States, where it is available as a generic, and in most other countries.[1][12] It is on the WADA prohibited list because of the possibility that it masks other substances, which makes it relevant to drug-tested physique and strength sports.[1]

Furosemide has a long-running place in looksmax.org threads under names such as the 'hollow cheek pill'. Guides and experience reports appeared in 2022 and 2023 and were revisited by a 2026 poster who said earlier guides were out of date.[22][16][17] Threads cover whether pet-medication listings are a route to supply, which members themselves note is inconsistent with prescription rules for humans, and where people in various countries obtain it.[18] Other threads compare it with eplerenone, with hydrochlorothiazide (which one poster calls a safer alternative) and with tretinoin as appearance tools.[19][20][23]

On T Nation, furosemide appears mostly in posts from patients who take it for heart conditions and describe its effects on daily life, such as constant urination and trouble staying hydrated; occasional remarks refer to bodybuilders who use diuretics for conditioning.[13][25][32]

Ongoing registered work includes a trial of self-administered subcutaneous Lasix for worsening heart failure, with enrolment starting in November 2025.[30] For bodybuilders, authors of peak-week and kidney reviews call for more study of water-manipulation practices and of subclinical kidney changes, which have rarely been investigated.[15] No published trial has tested furosemide for cosmetic facial slimming.

Human trials concern medical populations. Acute decompensated heart failure: DOSE (308 patients, bolus versus infusion and low versus high dose), CLOROTIC (add-on hydrochlorothiazide), and the TRANSFORM-HF comparison of torsemide and furosemide on mortality.[10][9][5] Meta-analyses have examined furosemide with albumin and with hypertonic saline.[3][4] A randomised trial in patients with chronic kidney disease having cardiac angiography compared saline, mannitol and furosemide for protecting renal function against radiocontrast agents.[11] Postpartum, preterm-infant and SIAD trials are listed above.[7][28][8][29] No studies found of furosemide for cosmetic facial or physique outcomes in healthy people.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org furosemide is discussed as a rapid facial 'debloat', with guides, experience threads and before-and-after posts; on T Nation it appears mostly in patient discussions with occasional mentions of physique use.[16][22][24][13]

claims.claim: Furosemide gives 'hollow cheeks' within hours by removing facial water.
claims.believers: A 2026 poster at about 8% body fat reports cheeks 'caving in' within an hour and a drawn eye area, and says it works.[16]
claims.experts: The label states that furosemide causes profound diuresis in excessive amounts and requires medical supervision; the change reflects fluid loss.[12][1]

claims.claim: It is only worthwhile for people who are already lean.
claims.believers: The same poster says users should be below about 15% body fat to see a benefit.[16]
claims.experts: No studies have examined facial appearance after furosemide in lean or other healthy people.

claims.claim: Fasting and exercise before taking it enhance the effect.
claims.believers: Posters describe fasting and training beforehand to lower sodium and, in their view, deepen the debloat.[17]
claims.experts: Peak-week reviews describe water, sodium and carbohydrate manipulation as widely practised with scarce supporting evidence.[15]

claims.believers: A thread title and discussion propose hydrochlorothiazide as a gentler option for the same debloat.[19]
claims.experts: Both drugs are prescription diuretics that cause electrolyte disturbances; hydrochlorothiazide has been combined with furosemide in heart-failure trials rather than compared for appearance.[9][1]

claims.claim: Pet-medication listings are an easy way to get it.
claims.believers: Members discuss veterinary tablets as a workaround for the prescription requirement, with others calling the situation absurd.[18]
claims.experts: Furosemide is prescription-only for people in the US and most countries; veterinary use is for horses, dogs and cats.[1][12]

claims.claim: Bodybuilders routinely 'DNP and Lasix' their way to a shredded look.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster refers to people who do this to manipulate the body.[13]
claims.experts: Reviews list diuretic misuse among practices with potential kidney risk, and the label warns of electrolyte depletion.[15][12]
